Teaching medical students to investigate medication errors can indeed have a positive impact on their attitudes towards patient safety. An active learning curriculum integrated into a clinical clerkship, as mentioned in the retrieved match, has been found relevant and recommended by students themselves. This suggests that such an approach can make learners more aware of the importance of patient safety and motivated to take steps to improve it.

By incorporating medication error investigation into their medical education, students may become more attentive to potential risks and adverse events associated with medications, leading them to adopt a more vigilant and proactive attitude towards patient safety. This, in turn, can help shape their long-term attitudes and behaviors regarding patient care.

Furthermore, students who are able to identify and address medication errors through investigation may develop a greater appreciation for the complexities of medical practice and the need for close monitoring and quality control measures. This increased awareness and commitment to patient safety can ultimately contribute to improved patient outcomes and better healthcare delivery.

In conclusion, teaching medical students to investigate medication errors is an effective way to change their attitudes towards patient safety, as evidenced by student feedback in the retrieved match. By integrating such an approach into their education, medical educators can empower future physicians with the knowledge, skills, and mindset necessary to prioritize patient safety above all else.
